title: Attention Is All You Need | p. 1 | Aa

passage: dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely
text:
The phrase means the Transformer drops both recurrent and convolutional layers entirely, relying only on attention. It is a claim about architecture, stated in the abstract.

Recurrence refers to networks such as LSTMs that process a sequence one step at a time, each step feeding into the next p. 1. Convolutions slide small filters over local windows of the input. By dispensing with both, the authors mean every position in the sequence is connected to every other through attention in a fixed number of operations, which is what makes the model parallelizable p. 6.

Here the phrase is the central design choice that the rest of the paper builds on. The introduction explains that sequential computation remains the fundamental constraint of recurrent models, and the Transformer is proposed as a way around it p. 2.

passage: This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples
text:
The passage says that the step-by-step nature of recurrent models prevents their computations from being run in parallel within a single training example.

The sentence refers back to the preceding description: a recurrent model generates each hidden state h_t as a function of the previous hidden state h_{t-1} and the input at position t. Because each state needs the one before it, the computation must proceed in order, one position after another. The authors note that this becomes critical for longer sequences, since memory limits also restrict how many examples can be batched together p. 2.

The word "precludes" simply means "rules out" or "makes impossible." Here the claim is that the sequential dependency is built into the architecture itself, so parallelization across positions within one example is not available to these models. This motivation is what the Transformer later sets out to remove by relying entirely on attention p. 2.

question: Why would large dot products push the softmax into regions with tiny gradients?
text:
The document gives the setup in footnote 4 but not the full explanation, so the second half of this is from general knowledge.

What the document says: if the components of q and k are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has mean 0 and variance dk p. 4. So as dk grows, the typical size of a dot product grows too (its standard deviation is √dk). That is why the authors divide by √dk, which brings the variance back to about 1.

Why that hurts the softmax (from general knowledge): softmax exponentiates its inputs, so when one score is much larger than the others, nearly all the weight goes to that one position. The output becomes almost one-hot, close to 0 for most entries and close to 1 for one. In that saturated region, the softmax's derivative is the weight times (1 minus the weight), which is near zero for both extremes. Changing the inputs slightly barely changes the output, so the gradient flowing back to the queries and keys is extremely small and learning stalls.

The paper only states this as a suspicion ("We suspect"), not something it tests directly.

Before you start
×

The paper proposes the Transformer, a translation architecture built only on attention, with no recurrence or convolution. It matters because it aims for better quality and far faster parallel training, and the rest of the paper describes, motivates and tests that design.

Key claims

1
The Transformer relies entirely on attention to draw global dependencies between input and output, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions. p. 2
2
Self-attention relates any two positions in a constant number of sequential operations, versus O(n) for recurrent layers. p. 6
3
The big model reaches 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German, beating prior results including ensembles by over 2 BLEU. p. 8
4
Ablations show single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, and quality also drops with too many heads. p. 9
5
A 4-layer Transformer with little task-specific tuning performs well on English constituency parsing, including with only 40K WSJ training sentences. p. 10

Keep in mind

The English-to-French big model score appears as 41.8 in the abstract and Table 2 but as 41.0 in the text of section 6.1. Check which figure you rely on.
Attention itself is not new. The novelty claimed is using it without recurrent or convolutional layers, so read the Background section with that distinction in mind.
Perplexities in Table 3 are per-wordpiece under byte-pair encoding, so they should not be compared with per-word perplexities from other work. Training cost figures are estimates built from GPU time and assumed sustained TFLOPS.

question: What limitations of the Transformer do the authors themselves acknowledge?
text:
Four sets of results stand out, all on the English-to-German development set p. 9.

First, the heads in rows (A). With computation held constant, a single head scores 24.9 BLEU against 25.8 for the base setting, which the authors call 0.9 BLEU worse. Quality also falls with 32 heads (25.4), so the benefit of multi-head attention is real but has a sweet spot p. 9. This is the direct test of the design choice the paper leans on most.

Second, the key size in rows (B). Cutting dk to 16 or 32 lowers BLEU to 25.1 and 25.4. The authors read this as a sign that dot-product compatibility may be too simple p. 9.

Third, size and dropout in rows (C) and (D). Bigger models help, for example dmodel 1024 reaches 26.0 and dff 4096 reaches 26.2. Removing dropout drops BLEU to 24.6 and perplexity rises to 5.77, so dropout matters for avoiding over-fitting p. 9. The label for each (D) row is incomplete, so I am inferring from the order that the dropout rows come first and the label-smoothing rows second. Label smoothing of 0.0 gives the best perplexity (4.67) but a lower BLEU (25.3), matching the paper's remark that smoothing hurts perplexity but improves BLEU p. 8.

Fourth, row (E). Learned positional embeddings give 25.7 BLEU against 25.8, nearly identical, so the sinusoidal choice is justified mainly by possible extrapolation to longer sequences, not by measured gains p. 6.

The limitations question was answered above.
